lessons.title: Why marriage at all
lessons.intro: Why Islam encourages marriage, how a marriage is made, and what to say to a couple who have just married.

steps.title: A promise, not just a party
body: Marriage is one of the oldest human ways of building a home. In Islam it is more than a celebration or a paper. It is a promise made before Allah, and a way for two people to care for each other, for children, and for a wider family.

In this lesson you will learn why Islam encourages marriage, what makes a Muslim marriage valid, and what to say to a couple who have just married. It is written for everyone: married, engaged, hoping to marry one day, or a parent or grown child helping someone else. No earlier knowledge is needed.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.title: Calm, affection and mercy
body: Allah says that one of His signs is that He made mates for us from among ourselves, so that we find calm in them, and that He placed between spouses affection and mercy. The ayah ends by saying this is for people who think.

Three words are worth knowing. Sukun is calm: a person you can rest next to. Mawaddah is warm affection that shows in what a person does. Rahmah is mercy: patience with faults and care when the other is weak, tired or in the wrong. A marriage is meant to grow all three.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: A solemn covenant
body: In another place the Qur’an calls the marriage bond a solemn covenant: a heavy, serious promise (4:21). That one word tells you how Islam sees it. It is not a casual deal that anyone can drop when it becomes difficult, and it is not an ownership of one person by another. It is a promise to treat each other well.
The next ayah is about living together. It tells husbands to live with their wives in kindness, and adds that you may dislike something in a person while Allah has placed much good in it (4:19).
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The call to marry
body: Islam does not ask believers to give up family life in order to worship more. In Bukhari 5063, three men heard how the Prophet ﷺ worshipped and each decided to go further: one would pray all night forever, one would fast every day, one would never marry. The Prophet ﷺ told them that he is the most conscious of Allah among them, yet he fasts and breaks his fast, sleeps, and marries; whoever turns away from his way is not one of his followers.

He also spoke to young people directly. He said that whoever among them is able to marry should marry, because it helps to lower the gaze and guard modesty, and whoever is not able should fast, because fasting protects (Bukhari 5066). The Qur’an says to help the unmarried among you to marry, and that if they are poor Allah will enrich them from His bounty (24:32).
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Is marriage required?
steps.intro: Scholars describe the ruling on marriage by a person’s situation, and the schools word it a little differently.

rows.name: A person who wants to marry and can afford it
rows.text: Hanafi and Hanbali: a recommended sunnah. Maliki: recommended for most people. Shafi’i: permissible in itself, and recommended for someone who wants it and has the means.

rows.name: A person who fears falling into sin and can afford to marry
rows.text: All four schools: marriage becomes obligatory for this person.

rows.name: A person who cannot support a spouse
rows.text: Do not rush. The Qur’an tells those who cannot find the means to marry to stay chaste until Allah enriches them (24:33), and the Prophet ﷺ advised fasting (Bukhari 5066).

rows.name: A person who would wrong a spouse
rows.text: Scholars say it is disliked, and in some cases forbidden, for this person to marry until they can treat a spouse justly.

steps.closing: If you are unsure which describes you, ask a trusted imam or teacher. It is a personal question and the answer depends on your life.
steps.review: The ruling on marriage by situation and the wording per school (Hanafi/Hanbali sunnah, Maliki recommended for most, Shafi’i permissible/recommended for the one who wants it). Written from general knowledge of the fiqh manuals, not checked against a primary text here. Needs a scholar.

steps.title: How a marriage is made
steps.intro: This is the simple outline. The details of the contract differ a little between the schools, and the next table shows where.

steps.detail: The Prophet ﷺ said that a woman who has been married before is not given in marriage until she is consulted, and a woman who has not is not given until her permission is asked. People asked how a young woman gives permission, and he said: by her silence (Bukhari 5136). A marriage is not something done to a person.
The mahr is a gift from the groom to the bride. It is hers (Qur’an 4:4). It can be money or something else of value, and the couple agree it together. It is not a price paid for her.

steps.text: The contract is spoken, with a guardian and witnesses.
steps.detail: Most schools require the bride’s guardian (wali) and two witnesses. See the table after this step for where the schools differ.

steps.text: Make it known, and hold a meal.
steps.detail: When Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf married, the Prophet ﷺ told him to hold a wedding meal even if it was only one sheep (Bukhari 5167). The meal is simple. It can be small.
Friends and family say a short blessing. You will learn it in the next step.

mistakes: Treating the wedding as the marriage. The wedding is one day. The marriage is the promise that follows it.
Making the mahr or the party so costly that it delays people from marrying.
Arranging a marriage for someone without asking them.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: What to say to a newly married couple
steps.label: [Established]
steps.note: When the Prophet ﷺ congratulated a man on his marriage, this is what he said. You can say it to a friend or relative after the contract or at the wedding. Read it slowly, one word at a time. There is no recording of this one in the app yet, because only the Qur’an has recordings here.

steps.title: Where the schools differ on the contract
steps.intro: All four schools agree that a valid marriage needs the bride’s consent, a mahr, and that it is made openly. They differ on these details.

rows.name: The guardian (wali)
rows.text: Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali: a woman’s marriage needs her guardian. They rely on reports such as Abu Dawud 2085 and Tirmidhi 1101 (graded sahih by al-Albani). Hanafi (the view of Abu Hanifa): an adult woman of sound mind may contract her own marriage, though involving her guardian is strongly encouraged.

rows.name: Witnesses
rows.text: Hanafi, Shafi’i and Hanbali: two witnesses must be present when the contract is made. Maliki: the marriage must be made public, and witnesses are needed at the latest before the couple live together.

rows.name: The least mahr
rows.text: Hanafi: at least ten dirhams. Maliki: at least a quarter of a dinar (about three dirhams). Shafi’i and Hanbali: no fixed minimum.

steps.closing: A couple should follow the practice of their own school or of the imam who marries them, and be sure the paperwork required by the country they live in is done too.
steps.source: Abu Dawud 2085 (graded sahih by al-Albani); Tirmidhi 1101 (graded sahih by al-Albani)
steps.review: Every row of this table (wali, witnesses, minimum mahr per school) is written from general fiqh knowledge and has not been checked against the manuals. Needs a scholar to confirm each school’s wording.

steps.title: What a marriage asks of both people
body: A marriage is not a place where one person is served and the other serves. The measure the Prophet ﷺ gave (next lesson) is how good you are to your family, and the Qur’an tells spouses to deal with each other in kindness.

Marriage is also never a licence to harm. The Qur’an forbids keeping a spouse in order to harm them (2:231). If you are being hurt, in body or in spirit, you are not asked to put up with it quietly. Safety comes first. Talk to a trusted imam, a counsellor, a doctor, or a helpline in your country. In an emergency, call the emergency number.
steps.label: [Established]

items.q: Which three gifts does Allah say He places between spouses?

options.text: Calm, affection and mercy
Wealth, beauty and fame
options.reteach: No. The ayah names calm (sukun), affection (mawaddah) and mercy (rahmah). They are things of the heart that grow with kindness.

options.text: Obedience, silence and patience
options.reteach: No. Those are not the three named. Allah names calm, affection and mercy, and they belong to both spouses.

items.explain: Qur’an 30:21: calm in each other, and affection and mercy placed between them.

items.q: What does the Qur’an call the marriage bond in 4:21?

options.text: A business deal
options.reteach: No. The Qur’an uses a much heavier word: a solemn covenant, a serious promise.

options.text: A private matter that needs no promise
options.reteach: No. It is a covenant: the promise is the heart of it.

options.text: A solemn covenant

items.explain: Marriage is called a solemn covenant, so it is to be kept with care.

items.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ tell the three men who wanted to give up marriage so they could worship more?

options.text: That he prays and sleeps, fasts and breaks his fast, and marries, and whoever turns away from his way is not one of his followers
That they were right, and he praised them
options.reteach: No. He told them his own way includes marrying, and that turning away from it is not his path.

options.text: He said nothing about it
options.reteach: He did answer them. The report is in Bukhari 5063: he fasts and breaks, sleeps, prays and marries.

items.explain: Bukhari 5063. Family life is part of the Prophet’s way, not a distraction from worship.
items.scenario: Three men decide to give up sleeping, eating by day, and marrying so that they can worship more.

items.q: What does the Prophet ﷺ teach about a woman’s agreement to marriage?

options.text: She must be asked, and her silence can be her agreement
Her family can decide for her without asking
options.reteach: No. In Bukhari 5136 the Prophet ﷺ said she is not given in marriage until her permission is asked.

options.text: Her agreement matters only the second time she marries
options.reteach: No. The report says a previously married woman must be consulted and a woman not married before must give her permission.

items.explain: Bukhari 5136: a woman is asked, and the people were told that her silence is her permission.

steps.prompt: Put the main moments of a marriage in order.

items.why: Everything starts with their own agreement. Nobody is married without it.
The couple usually settle the gift to the bride before or at the contract.

items.text: The contract is spoken with the guardian and witnesses
items.why: This is the moment the marriage begins, in front of the people who are needed (details depend on the school).

items.text: Friends and family say the blessing
items.why: They congratulate the couple with the words the Prophet ﷺ used.
The Prophet ﷺ told Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf to hold a meal, even a simple one.

steps.explain: The marriage begins with free agreement and a spoken contract. The blessing and the meal come when it is made public.

steps.prompt: Match the word to its meaning. Tap one on the left, then its meaning on the right.

right.text: Calm: someone you can rest beside

pairs.why: Sukun is calm. It is the first gift Allah names in 30:21.

right.text: Warm affection shown in what you do

pairs.why: Mawaddah is warm love that shows in actions.

right.text: Mercy: patience with faults and care in weakness

pairs.why: Rahmah is mercy. It is what keeps a marriage going when one person is tired or in the wrong.

right.text: The bride’s gift from the groom, and it is hers

pairs.why: The mahr belongs to the bride (4:4).

right.text: The bride’s guardian in the contract

pairs.why: The wali is the bride’s guardian. Three schools require one; the Hanafi school allows an adult woman to contract herself.

items.q: Who does the mahr belong to?

options.text: Her father
options.reteach: No. The mahr is the bride’s own gift (4:4). It does not go to her family.

options.text: The bride
The groom’s family
options.reteach: No. It comes from the groom to the bride. It is hers.

items.explain: The mahr is the bride’s. It is a gift, not a price.

items.q: Which word completes the blessing for a newly married couple? It asks Allah to bring them together in ____.

options.text: maal
options.reteach: Maal means wealth. The blessing asks for something more lasting: that they be brought together in good (khayr).

options.text: khayr
dunyaa
options.reteach: Dunyaa means this world. The word in the blessing is khayr: good.

items.explain: The blessing ends: wa jama’a baynakuma fee khayr: and may He bring you both together in good.

items.q: Which is true about the guardian (wali) in the marriage contract?

options.text: All four schools say exactly the same
options.reteach: No. They differ here, and the table shows how. None of them is a mistake to correct in another Muslim.

options.text: The schools differ: three require a guardian, and the Hanafi school allows an adult woman to contract her own marriage
No school speaks of a guardian at all
options.reteach: They all speak of it. The schools that require a guardian rely on the Prophet’s words that there is no marriage without a guardian.

items.explain: Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali require a guardian; Hanafi scholars allow an adult woman to contract her own marriage.

items.q: What should this student do?

options.text: Keep chaste, fast, and ask Allah to enrich them, rather than rushing into something they cannot carry
Marry now and think about money later, whatever happens
options.reteach: The Qur’an (24:33) tells those who cannot find the means to wait until Allah enriches them, and the Prophet ﷺ advised fasting.

options.text: Stop caring about faith altogether
options.reteach: No. Allah and His Messenger ﷺ give a way for exactly this situation: patience, fasting, and trust.

items.scenario: A student wants to marry, but cannot yet support a family and is finding it hard to stay patient.

items.q: A person in a marriage is being hurt. What does Islam ask of them?

options.text: To stay quiet no matter what happens
options.reteach: No. 2:231 forbids keeping a spouse in order to harm them. You are not asked to be silent about harm.

options.text: Safety comes first: keeping a spouse to harm them is forbidden, and they should seek a trusted imam, counsellor or helpline
Nothing can be done
options.reteach: Something can: talk to a trusted imam, a counsellor or a helpline, and in an emergency call the emergency number.

items.explain: Qur’an 2:231 forbids harm. Seeking help is right, not shameful.
items.scenario: Someone tells you that a spouse has been hurting them, and asks if they must just endure it.

steps.title: Ask Hādi a question about marriage
steps.body: Is there something about marriage you have wondered about: the mahr, the contract, what to say to a couple? Ask Hādi. Every answer shows where it comes from.

steps.title: What you can now do
canDo: Name the three gifts Allah places between spouses, and what each means.
Say why Islam encourages marriage, and what the Prophet ﷺ told the three men.
Outline how a marriage is made, and say where the schools differ.
Say the blessing for a newly married couple, with its meaning.
Say where to turn if a marriage is causing harm.

lessons.title: The best of you
lessons.intro: The Prophet’s measure of a good person, how he lived it at home, and small habits that make a home kinder.

steps.title: Who are you at home?
body: Many of us keep our best manners for visitors, colleagues and strangers, and give our family what is left over: the tired, short-tempered version of ourselves.

Islam turns that around. The question is not only how you behave in the mosque or at work. It is how you behave in the kitchen, in the car and at the end of a long day, with the people who cannot leave.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.title: The best of you
body: Aisha reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: the best of you is the one who is best to his family, and I am the best of you to my family. The word he used for family is ahl, the people of your household.

This is a measure of goodness that cannot be faked, because your family sees you when you are not performing. A person can pray long, speak well and be generous in public, and still fall short of this measure.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Tirmidhi 3895 (graded sahih by al-Albani, hasan by Darussalam)

steps.title: A race on a journey
body: Aisha told this about the Prophet ﷺ. She was travelling with him and raced him on foot, and she won. Later, when she had put on some weight, they raced again, and he won. He said to her: this one is for that one.

It is a small, laughing moment, and it was kept and told for centuries because it shows how he was with his wife: he played with her, he remembered a joke from long before, and he did not need to win.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: He noticed her mood
body: The Prophet ﷺ once told Aisha: I know when you are pleased with me and when you are angry with me. She asked how. He said that when she was pleased she would say, no, by the Lord of Muhammad, and when she was angry she would say, no, by the Lord of Ibrahim. She answered: yes, but I only leave out your name.
Look at what he did. He paid attention to her feelings, and he said it with a smile instead of a complaint. Noticing is a gift you can give a family member every day.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Kindness, and a smile
body: The Qur’an tells husbands to live with their wives in kindness, and gives a reason that is easy to remember: you may dislike something in a person, and Allah may have placed a great deal of good in it (4:19).

The Prophet ﷺ also said that smiling in the face of your brother is charity (Tirmidhi 1956, graded sahih by al-Albani). That hadith speaks of every fellow Muslim. It certainly includes the ones you live with.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: What a wife is owed
body: A man asked the Prophet ﷺ what the right of a wife is over her husband. He answered: that you feed her when you eat, that you clothe her when you clothe yourself, that you do not strike her face, that you do not insult her, and that you do not keep away from her except inside the house.

In plain words: provide for her at the level you live at, speak to her with respect, and if you are angry and need distance, do not send her away or leave. This report is about the husband’s duties because the question was about them. The next lesson is about mercy running both ways.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Abu Dawud 2142 (graded hasan sahih by al-Albani)
steps.review: The plain-words paraphrase of "do not keep away from her except inside the house" (do not send her away or leave) is the app author’s reading. Please confirm the wording.

steps.title: Anger and the hands
body: Aisha reported that the Prophet ﷺ never struck anyone with his hand, neither a woman nor a servant, except when fighting in the cause of Allah (Muslim 2328). He also told people who are quarrelling to avoid striking the face (Muslim 2612).

Some people use a verse about disagreement between spouses (4:34) to excuse harsh treatment at home. Scholars have read that verse in different ways, and this lesson does not try to settle it. What is clear is the Prophet’s own example: he never struck a woman. Nothing in Islam allows injuring, shaming or frightening a spouse, and the best of the believers are the best to their families.
If you are on the receiving end of this, it is not your fault, and you do not have to put up with it. See the safety note in the last lesson, and talk to someone you trust.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: This step mentions Qur’an 4:34 without giving a ruling and says no scholar permits injuring or shaming a spouse. Needs a scholar to confirm the wording and balance.

steps.title: Seven small habits for a kinder home
steps.intro: None of these needs money or a special occasion. Pick one and do it this week.

steps.detail: The Prophet ﷺ called a smile charity (Tirmidhi 1956, graded sahih by al-Albani).

steps.text: Notice something, and say it kindly.
steps.detail: Like the Prophet ﷺ did with Aisha: "I can tell you are tired" is a better start than "what is wrong with you?"

steps.text: Say thank you for ordinary things.
steps.detail: The meal, the washing, the work. Small thanks stop small resentments growing.

steps.text: Listen to the end before you answer.
steps.detail: Put the phone down. Let the other person finish.
Laugh, walk, race. The Prophet ﷺ did (Abu Dawud 2578, graded sahih by al-Albani).
If you say "I will call at six", call at six.
You do not have to be wrong in every way. You can still be sorry that it hurt.

steps.label: [Reflection]
steps.source: Tirmidhi 1956 (graded sahih by al-Albani); Abu Dawud 2578 (graded sahih by al-Albani)

items.q: According to the hadith, who are the best of people?

options.text: Those who are best to their families
Those who pray the longest
options.reteach: Prayer matters a great deal, but this hadith measures goodness by how you treat your family.

options.text: Those who earn the most
options.reteach: No. Wealth is not the measure here. The Prophet ﷺ said the best of you is the best to his family.

items.explain: The best of you is the best to his family (Tirmidhi 3895, graded sahih by al-Albani).

items.q: What does this hadith say about this person?

options.text: Work manners matter more than home manners
options.reteach: The hadith says the opposite: the family sees you with nothing to prove.

options.text: Home life is private, so it does not count
options.reteach: It counts. The Prophet ﷺ set the test at home.

options.text: Real goodness shows at home first

items.explain: The best of you is the best to his family: so a person who is warm outside and harsh at home has missed the measure.
items.scenario: A man is polite and patient with everyone at work, and sharp and impatient with his family.

items.q: What does the story of Aisha’s race show?

options.text: The Prophet ﷺ played and joked with his wife
He never joked at home
options.reteach: No. Abu Dawud 2578 (graded sahih by al-Albani) shows him racing her and laughing about it years later.

options.text: Races are only for men
options.reteach: No. Aisha raced the Prophet ﷺ, twice, on a journey.

items.explain: They raced twice, she won once and he won once, and he said: this one is for that one.

items.q: In Bukhari 6114, who does the Prophet ﷺ call strong?

options.text: The one who controls himself when angry
The one who wins every fight
options.reteach: No. He said the strong one is not the one who overcomes people by strength.

options.text: The one who never feels anger
options.reteach: No. Anger is a feeling. The strong one is the one who controls himself while angry.

items.explain: The strong one is the one who controls himself in anger (Bukhari 6114).

steps.prompt: Your anger is rising in the middle of an argument. Put these steps in the order that helps most.

items.text: Notice the anger and stop talking
items.why: Words said in anger are the ones that leave marks. The strong one is the one who controls himself (Bukhari 6114).

items.text: Sit down; if it stays, lie down
items.why: The Prophet ﷺ told an angry person standing to sit, and if the anger stays, to lie down (Abu Dawud 4782, graded sahih by al-Albani).

items.text: Ask Allah for help and calm down
items.why: Say a short du’a or make wudu. When you are calm, you can think about what you want to say.

items.text: Come back and say what hurt, kindly
items.why: Talk about the problem, not about the other person’s whole character.
Even if the other person was also wrong, apologising for your own part ends arguments.

steps.explain: First stop. Then change your position. Then calm yourself. Then speak kindly and take responsibility for your part.

steps.prompt: Match each story or saying to what it teaches. Tap one on the left, then its meaning on the right.

right.text: Play and laughter belong in a marriage

pairs.why: The Prophet ﷺ raced his wife and laughed about it.

left.text: By the Lord of Muhammad, by the Lord of Ibrahim

right.text: Noticing a family member’s mood, and saying it kindly

pairs.why: He noticed her mood from a small change in her words.

left.text: Sit down; if it stays, lie down

right.text: What to do when anger comes while you are standing

pairs.why: It is the Prophet’s advice for anger.

left.text: Never struck a woman or a servant

right.text: The Prophet’s own practice at home

pairs.why: Aisha reported it (Muslim 2328).

right.text: A small act that counts as charity

pairs.why: Smiling in your brother’s face is charity.

items.q: Which of these is part of what the Prophet ﷺ said a wife is owed?

options.text: To be kept away from her own family
options.reteach: No. That is not in the report. Abu Dawud 2142 (graded hasan sahih by al-Albani) lists food, clothing, no insulting and no striking the face.

options.text: To be fed and clothed as her husband is
To stay silent when there is a disagreement
options.reteach: No. The report asks the husband to speak with respect and not to insult.

items.explain: Feed her as you eat, clothe her as you clothe yourself, do not insult her, do not strike her face, and do not keep away from her except inside the house.

items.q: You are angry and standing in the kitchen after a bad day. What does the Prophet ﷺ advise?

options.text: Walk out and slam the door
options.reteach: No. Leaving in a rage makes things worse. The Prophet ﷺ told an angry person to sit, and to lie down if it remains.

options.text: Sit down, and if the anger stays, lie down
Say everything now so it is out
options.reteach: No. Words said in anger leave marks. Stop and control yourself first.

items.scenario: You are standing in the kitchen, very angry about something your spouse said.

items.q: What did Aisha report about the Prophet ﷺ and striking?

options.text: He struck only when he was angry
options.reteach: No. She said he never struck a woman or servant at all. The report is Muslim 2328.

options.text: He never struck anyone with his hand, neither a woman nor a servant, except when fighting in the cause of Allah
Nothing is reported about it
options.reteach: It is reported in Muslim 2328.

items.q: Your spouse comes home tired and quiet. Which is closer to the way the Prophet ﷺ treated Aisha?

options.text: Notice it kindly and ask, or help
Ignore it and keep watching the screen
options.reteach: The Prophet ﷺ noticed Aisha’s mood from a few words. Noticing is part of the way.

options.text: Say their mood is annoying
options.reteach: That would add to the weight. The Prophet ﷺ noticed and spoke with warmth.

items.explain: Bukhari 5228: he noticed, and he said it with a smile.
items.scenario: Your spouse comes in and sits down without saying much.

items.q: What does the Prophet ﷺ say about smiling at a fellow Muslim?

options.text: It is a sin if it is too wide
options.reteach: No. There is no such rule. He called a smile charity.

options.text: It is charity
It has no value in Islam
options.reteach: It does. He called it charity (Tirmidhi 1956, graded sahih by al-Albani).

items.explain: Your smiling in the face of your brother is charity.

steps.body: Choose one of the seven habits and do it today. If you want help with the words for a sincere apology, ask Hādi.

canDo: Say the hadith that measures goodness by how you treat your family.
Tell two short stories of how the Prophet ﷺ was with his wife.

Name one small habit you will start this week.

lessons.title: Mercy between you
lessons.intro: Covering faults, settling quarrels, getting fair help, and knowing when to seek safety.

steps.title: The same quarrel, every week
body: Most arguments at home are small: who was supposed to do what, a tone of voice, a forgotten message. The trouble is not that there is a disagreement. The trouble is what we do with it.
In this lesson you will learn what the Qur’an and the Prophet ﷺ say about covering faults, settling quarrels, getting fair help when you are stuck, and how long a silence may last.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.title: Clothing for each other
body: The Qur’an says of spouses: they are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them. The ayah speaks about the nights of Ramadan, and the picture is easy to understand. A garment is close to the body, it covers, it protects, and it warms.
Scholars take from this image that spouses cover one another’s faults and protect one another, rather than exposing each other.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: The explanation of the garment image (closeness, covering, protection) is the app author’s summary of standard commentary. Please confirm.

steps.title: Cover, and do not broadcast
body: The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah will conceal on the Day of Resurrection the faults of the person who conceals the faults of others in this world (Muslim 2590). He also said that whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should say what is good or stay quiet (Bukhari 6018).

At home this means: do not use your spouse’s faults as stories to tell your friends, do not post about them, and do not bring up an old mistake to win a new argument. If you need advice, take it to one fair, trusted person, not to an audience.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: When you cannot settle it alone
body: The Qur’an says that if a couple fear a break between them, a fair person from his side and a fair person from her side should be sent to them. If both want peace, Allah will bring it about between them (4:35). Another ayah says that settling between them is best (4:128).
So there is a step between silence and separation: ask a fair, wise and trusted person from each family, or an imam or counsellor, to help you talk.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The Prophet listened to his wife
body: At Hudaybiyyah, after the peace treaty was written, the Prophet ﷺ told the Companions three times to get up, sacrifice their animals and shave their heads. None of them moved. He went to his wife Umm Salama and told her what had happened.
She advised him to go out and say nothing to anyone, but to sacrifice and call the barber himself. He did, and when the people saw it they stood up and did the same.
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked for his wife’s advice in a hard moment and acted on it. A good family takes counsel from each other.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: When you disagree: five steps
steps.intro: These are practical suggestions based on the Qur’an and Sunnah. Use them as a guide, not a script.

steps.detail: The strong one is the one who controls himself in anger (Bukhari 6114). If you need to, sit down first.

steps.text: Talk about the problem, not the person.
steps.detail: "I felt hurt when the plans changed" opens a door. "You always..." closes it.
Repeat back what you heard before you reply.

steps.text: Own your part and say sorry.
steps.detail: Even when you were only partly wrong.

The Prophet ﷺ said it is not lawful for a Muslim to desert a brother for more than three nights, and the better one is the one who greets first (Bukhari 6077). The report speaks of Muslims in general; the same spirit applies at home.

mistakes: Bringing up old faults to win the new argument.
Going quiet for days to punish someone.
Telling the whole family your side before you have talked to your spouse.
steps.label: [Reflection]
steps.review: The use of the three-nights report for spouses is the app author’s application of its spirit. Needs a scholar to confirm the wording.

steps.title: When a marriage is in real trouble
body: Sometimes helping each other is not enough. Divorce is allowed in Islam, but it is a serious matter with detailed rules, and the schools differ in some of them. Do not take your rules from social media or from a friend. Ask a qualified imam.

Two things are certain. A spouse must not be kept in order to harm them (2:231). And a person who is being hurt in body or in spirit should get safe first, and then get help from a trusted imam, a counsellor or a helpline. In an emergency, call the emergency number.
steps.label: [Established]

lessons.title: The first teacher
lessons.intro: What the Qur’an and the Prophet ﷺ ask of us towards our parents, in hard times too, and after they have passed.

steps.title: Your first teachers
body: Before you could read, someone taught you to speak, to eat, and to say your first words. For most of us that someone was a parent.

The Qur’an puts the duty to parents straight after the duty to worship Allah alone. In this lesson you will learn what is asked of you, in plain words: what to do while your parents are alive, how to handle hard situations, and what you can still do for them after they have died. It is for anyone with parents, living or gone.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.title: Who is most deserving of my care?
body: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked: who among the people is most deserving of my good company? The Prophet ﷺ said: your mother. The man asked: and then who? He said: your mother. The man asked again: and then who? He said: your mother. The man asked a fourth time: and then who? He said: your father.

Notice the three. The Prophet ﷺ did not need long speeches. He repeated one word three times, and the father is named fourth. Scholars say this is because of what a mother goes through: pregnancy, birth and early care. Both parents are owed good treatment.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: She carried you
body: The Qur’an itself reminds us. Allah says that He has enjoined upon people care for their parents, that the mother carried the child in weakness upon weakness, and that the child is to be grateful to Allah and to the parents (31:14). In another ayah we are told she carried and delivered the child with hardship (46:15).
This is not said to make anyone feel guilty. It is a reminder, so that when your parent is slow, repeats a story or needs help, you remember who once did the same for you.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Not even “uff”
steps.label: [Established]
steps.note: Allah commands good treatment of parents, even when they are old and living with you. Do not say uff (a small sound of annoyance) and do not push them away; speak to them with a noble word. Then lower the wing of humility out of mercy, and make this du’a for them. Read the meaning under each line.

steps.title: Hear the du’a for your parents
steps.note: Listen to how the du’a is recited. The second half is the words to say for your parents. In the pause, say it after the reciter.

steps.title: Ways to honour your parents, now
steps.intro: You do not need to do all of these. Choose the ones that fit your parents and your life.

steps.text: Speak gently, and keep your voice low.
steps.detail: The Qur’an says not even uff (17:23). Take care with your tone, especially when you are tired.
A short call every day is worth more than a big visit once a year. Let them finish their sentence.
A lift to an appointment, shopping, fixing a tap, helping with a phone.
Use the du’a of 17:24 that you just read.

steps.text: Be kind to their friends and relatives.
steps.detail: The Prophet ﷺ said that the finest act of goodness is that a person treat kindly the loved ones of his father (Muslim 2552).

steps.text: Be patient when they are hard to be patient with.
steps.detail: Tiredness, memory, pain and fear can change a person. Do not take it as an attack.

mistakes: Talking about them with others in a way you would not say to their face.
Only visiting when you need something.
Thinking that good treatment means you must never disagree. You can disagree gently.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: When it is hard
body: Some parents are not Muslim. Some ask for things that are wrong. Some have been hard on their children. The Qur’an speaks to this directly. If they push you to join others with Allah in worship, do not obey them, but still keep them company in this world with appropriate kindness (31:15).

Asma bint Abu Bakr told the Prophet ﷺ that her mother, who was not a Muslim, had come to her and hoped for help. She asked if she should keep good relations with her. He said: yes, keep good relations with her (Bukhari 2620).

So the line is clear. You do not have to obey a command to do wrong. You are still asked to treat your parents with respect and kindness. If you are being harmed, be safe first, and ask a trusted imam or teacher how to balance respect and safety.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: After they have passed
body: The Prophet ﷺ said that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except for three: ongoing charity, knowledge that continues to benefit people, and a righteous child who prays for them (Muslim 1631).

When the mother of Sa’d ibn Ubada died, he asked the Prophet ﷺ whether it would benefit her if he gave charity on her behalf. The Prophet ﷺ said yes (Bukhari 2756). Many people give charity, help the poor, or fund water for their parents. A child’s du’a is also a gift. The Qur’an records the du’a of Nuh, which asks forgiveness for himself, his parents, and the believers (71:28).
steps.label: [Established]

lessons.title: Teaching the prayer
lessons.intro: What the Prophet ﷺ taught about children and prayer, what to make of the hard word in the hadith, and a gentle plan by age.

steps.title: Children learn by watching
body: Nobody learns to pray from a lecture. Children learn the prayer the way they learn to walk: by being near it, copying it, and being helped. The Prophet ﷺ taught the prayer the same way.

In this lesson you will learn what the Prophet ﷺ said about when to ask a child to pray, how he treated children in the prayer, and a gentle plan that fits each age. If you are the child, this will also explain why your parents ask what they ask.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.title: Enjoin your family to pray
body: Allah told His Messenger ﷺ to enjoin prayer upon his family and to be steadfast in it (20:132). Luqman told his son to establish prayer (31:17). Teaching the prayer begins with the parent doing it.

The Prophet ﷺ gave an age guide. Abdullah ibn Amr reported that he said: command your children to pray when they are seven years old, and beat them for it when they are ten years old, and separate them in their beds.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Qur'an 20:132; Qur'an 31:17; Abu Dawud 495 (graded hasan sahih by al-Albani)

steps.title: What does “beat” mean here?
body: The word in the hadith is a word for striking, and we should not hide that. But the Prophet ﷺ himself never struck a woman or a servant (Muslim 2328), and he told people to avoid the face when quarrelling (Muslim 2612).

Scholars who explain this hadith say it is about a ten-year-old who is not praying after three years of being taught, and that any striking is only a light tap meant to train, never in anger, never on the face, and never causing pain or a mark. Many teachers and scholars today say the better way is calm, firm discipline with no hitting at all, and that this fits the Prophet’s own example.
Three things are clear: the child is first taught gently; there is no excuse for violence; and if you fear you will lose your temper, do not touch the child at all.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Abu Dawud 495 (graded hasan sahih by al-Albani); Muslim 2328; Muslim 2612
steps.review: This step explains the word for striking in the 7/10-year hadith. It says classical scholars limit it to a light, non-harmful tap and that many modern scholars prefer no hitting. Needs a scholar to confirm the wording and attributions.

steps.title: Children near you in prayer
body: The Prophet ﷺ welcomed children in the prayer. He once prayed carrying his granddaughter Umama: when he prostrated he put her down, and when he stood he lifted her again (Bukhari 516). Another time one of his grandsons climbed on his back while he was prostrating, and he made the prostration long so as not to disturb him (Nasa’i 1141, graded sahih by al-Albani).
He also said that he sometimes begins a prayer meaning to make it long, but when he hears a child cry he shortens it, because he does not want to trouble the child’s mother (Bukhari 707).
So a child near you in prayer is welcome, not a problem to remove.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Bukhari 516; Nasa’i 1141 (graded sahih by al-Albani); Bukhari 707

steps.title: A gentle plan by age
steps.intro: This follows the hadith above and the practice of many teachers. Every child is different. Go at their pace.

steps.text: Under seven: let them be near you.
steps.detail: Let them stand beside you, copy you, and hear you recite. Do not correct every movement.

steps.text: Teach the words, one at a time.
steps.detail: Start with Allahu akbar, then the words of bowing and prostrating. Use the Path course lessons on wudu, the prayer and Al-Fatihah.

steps.text: At seven: ask them, kindly and every day, to pray.
steps.detail: Pray where they can see you, ask them to join, and sit with them after.

steps.text: At ten: be firmer, and keep calm.
steps.detail: Talk about it. Link it to things they care about, like screen time. Never shame them in front of others.
This is part of the same hadith. It is about modesty and growing up.

steps.text: At puberty: the prayer is required.
steps.detail: All four schools agree that prayer becomes obligatory when a person reaches puberty and is of sound mind. Until then the training prepares them.

mistakes: Making the prayer a punishment or a threat.
Correcting every mistake in front of other people.
Expecting a six-year-old to pray like an adult.
Not praying yourself.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Abu Dawud 495 (graded hasan sahih by al-Albani)
steps.review: The plan by age and the statement that all four schools agree prayer becomes obligatory at puberty are general teaching, not checked against the manuals. Please confirm.

lessons.title: Mercy, not severity
lessons.intro: How the Prophet ﷺ treated children, and a calm way to correct them when you are tired.

steps.title: A spill, a long day
body: It has been a long day. The milk goes over, the homework is not done, and your voice rises before you decide to raise it. Every parent knows this moment.
What does the Prophet ﷺ teach us for it? In this lesson: how he was with children, why kindness is worth more than harshness, and a calm way to correct a child when you are tired.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.title: He kissed his grandson
body: Abu Huraira told that the Prophet ﷺ kissed his grandson al-Hasan while al-Aqra’ ibn Habis was sitting there. Al-Aqra’ said: I have ten children and I have never kissed any of them. The Prophet ﷺ looked at him and said: whoever is not merciful will not be shown mercy.
A strong man had no habit of affection, and the Prophet ﷺ did not praise that. He told him mercy is something we are asked to show.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Kindness makes things beautiful
body: Aisha reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: kindness is not found in anything except that it adds to its beauty, and it is not taken out of anything except that it makes it defective (Muslim 2594). Another time he said that Allah is kind and gentle and loves kindness in all matters (Bukhari 6927).
For a parent, this means: when you must correct a child, how you do it matters as much as what you say.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Ten years, and never uff
body: Anas ibn Malik served the Prophet ﷺ for ten years, as a boy. He said that in all that time the Prophet ﷺ never said uff to him, and never asked him: why did you do that, or why did you not do that? (Bukhari 6038).
It does not mean there were no mistakes. It means that the way he corrected them left a child feeling safe, so that decades later Anas still spoke of him with love.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Be fair between your children
body: Nu’man ibn Bashir said that his father gave him a gift, and his mother asked the father to make the Prophet ﷺ a witness. The Prophet ﷺ asked: have you given the like of it to all your sons? The father said no. The Prophet ﷺ said: fear Allah, and be just to your children. The father went back and took the gift back (Bukhari 2587).
Children notice favouritism early, and it hurts. Treat them fairly in gifts and in attention, even though they are different.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: He greeted children
body: Anas once passed some boys, greeted them, and said that the Prophet ﷺ used to do this (Bukhari 6247). Greeting a child first tells them that they are a person who deserves respect, and it teaches them to greet.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: A calm way to correct a child
steps.intro: This is practical advice, in the spirit of the reports above. Adjust it to the age of your child.

steps.detail: Take a breath. If you are very angry, step out of the room for a minute. The strong one is the one who controls himself in anger (Bukhari 6114).
First: is anyone hurt?

steps.text: Say what happened in plain words.
steps.detail: "The milk spilled." Not "You are always careless."

steps.text: Ask for what you want next time.
steps.detail: "Next time, hold the glass with both hands."

steps.text: Let the child help put it right.
steps.detail: Wiping the table is a good lesson, and it keeps their dignity.
A hug, a smile. The Prophet ﷺ kissed his grandson. Correction should not end with distance.

mistakes: Shouting names such as lazy or stupid. Words stay inside a child.
Correcting in front of others.
Different rules every day, so the child cannot know what is expected.
Hitting. The Prophet ﷺ never struck a woman or servant (Muslim 2328).
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.title: If a child is in danger
body: Everything above is about ordinary mistakes. If a child is being hurt, in body or in spirit, they should be protected. A child who is being harmed should tell a trusted adult, such as a teacher, a doctor, or a relative, and in most countries there are child protection lines.
A parent who fears they might hurt a child in anger should step away from the child, call someone who can help, and seek support. Asking for help is a sign of strength.

lessons.title: The best provision
lessons.intro: What a parent gives that cannot be bought: manners, faith and du’a.

steps.title: More than food and school
body: A parent provides a lot: a bed, meals, school fees. But what a child carries into adult life is something else: how to talk, how to ask, how to pray, how to say sorry.
This lesson is about the provision that cannot be bought: manners, faith, and du’a, and how to give them to a child in small, daily ways.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.title: Protect your family
body: Allah tells the believers to protect themselves and their families from a Fire. The ayah is serious. It means that a parent’s duty is not only to the body, but to the direction of the family: toward Allah.
This is not a call to fear. It is a call to teach, with love, and above all by example.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Every one of you is a shepherd
body: Ibn Umar reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: every one of you is a shepherd and is responsible for his flock. A man is a guardian of his family and is responsible for them. A woman is a guardian of her husband’s house and is responsible for it.
The word shepherd is a kind one. A shepherd does not drive the flock with a stick: he guides, feeds, protects and knows each one. Both parents carry this duty.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: What you spend on your family
body: The Prophet ﷺ told Sa’d ibn Abi Waqqas that he would be rewarded for whatever he spent for the sake of Allah, even the morsel he put into his wife’s mouth (Bukhari 56). He also said that among all the dinars a person spends, the one with the greatest reward is the one spent on his family (Muslim 995).
Feeding, clothing, and educating your children with halal earnings is worship. It is not a lesser act than charity to strangers.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Luqman teaches his son
steps.label: [Established]
steps.note: Luqman is the Qur’an’s picture of a wise father. Read the five things he teaches his son: worship Allah alone, pray, do good and forbid wrong, be patient, do not be arrogant, and be moderate and lower your voice. Notice that he speaks to his son tenderly: O my son.

steps.title: Three small manners to teach

If you forget to say it at the start, say it when you remember (Abu Dawud 3767, graded sahih by al-Albani).
Greet children first, as the Prophet ﷺ did (Bukhari 6247), and teach them to greet.
The Prophet ﷺ taught: the one who sneezes says Alhamdulillah, the one who hears says Yarhamukallah, and the sneezer answers Yahdeekumullah wa yuslih balakum (Bukhari 6224).

lessons.title: Serving the family
lessons.intro: What the Prophet ﷺ did at home, how scholars speak about housework, and a way to share the load.

steps.title: Who washes the dishes?
body: In many homes the biggest arguments are not about faith. They are about dishes, laundry, and who did more today. This lesson looks at what the Prophet ﷺ did at home, and what that says about work at home and worship.
It is for anyone who lives with other people: spouses, parents, grown children, flatmates.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.title: What did he do at home?
body: Al-Aswad asked Aisha: what did the Prophet ﷺ use to do in his house? She said: he used to keep himself busy serving his family, and when it was time for prayer, he would go out for it.
The Messenger of Allah, the leader of the community, spent his time at home helping with the work of the house. Then, when the prayer was called, he went. Work at home and prayer were not enemies.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Home work can be worship
body: The Prophet ﷺ told Sa’d that what he spent on his family, even a morsel placed in his wife’s mouth, would be rewarded (Bukhari 56). If food is rewarded, so is the effort of cooking it, cleaning up after it, and serving those who eat it, when done with a sincere intention.
This does not mean the home is only for one person to work. It means no task at home is too small to count.
steps.label: [Interpretive]

steps.title: Is housework a duty?
steps.intro: Scholars have discussed this question. Here is a fair summary, and a note that you should ask a qualified scholar about your own case.
steps.agree: Everyone agrees on kindness and sharing.

rows.name: What is agreed
rows.text: The husband must provide food, clothing and a place to live. The Prophet ﷺ himself helped at home. Kindness and cooperation are encouraged by everyone.

rows.name: Some jurists
rows.text: Several classical jurists, commonly reported from the Hanafi, Shafi’i and Hanbali schools, say a wife is not legally obliged to do the housework, and that doing it is generosity.

rows.name: Other jurists
rows.text: Some, including many Maliki scholars, say it follows local custom: what is normal for a wife in that place and in her situation.

rows.name: What this means in practice
rows.text: Do not use the law as a stick. In a working household the practical answer is to talk, share the load, and treat each other as the Prophet ﷺ treated his family.

steps.closing: Learn what scholars say, then settle it with each other in kindness.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: Please confirm the summary of the schools’ views on a wife’s legal duty to do housework (Hanafi, Shafi’i, Hanbali, Maliki) and the wording of the practical note.

steps.title: Fatima and the grinding stone
body: Ali reported that Fatima, the Prophet’s daughter, suffered from grinding grain with the hand mill. When she heard that servants had come from the war gains, she went to ask her father for one, but did not find him, so she told Aisha.

When the Prophet ﷺ came, he visited them at night while they were in bed. He said: shall I tell you something better than what you asked? When you go to your beds, say Allahu akbar 34 times, alhamdulillah 33 times and subhanallah 33 times.
Notice that the Prophet ﷺ did not dismiss her hard work. He gave them something to carry them through the tiredness. Ali said he never missed it afterwards.

lessons.title: The family that prays
lessons.intro: Small habits that make a home a place of remembrance, and the hadith that encourage them.

steps.title: A house that remembers Allah
body: Some homes are quiet and some are loud. Few are a place where Allah is mentioned. This lesson is about small habits that make a home a place of remembrance: dhikr, night prayer, and the words when you enter.
You do not need a big plan. One small habit, done together, is a good beginning.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.title: The living and the dead
body: The Prophet ﷺ said that the example of the one who remembers his Lord, compared to the one who does not, is like a living creature compared to a dead one (Bukhari 6407).
The comparison is strong. A home that mentions Allah has life in it, even when it is poor or noisy.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Hearts find rest
steps.label: [Established]
steps.note: Allah says that hearts find peace through remembering Him. Read the meaning. This is why a family dhikr is not an extra: it is a source of calm for the whole home.

steps.title: Hear it recited
steps.note: Listen once, then say it after the reciter in the pause.

steps.title: When you enter your home
body: Jabir reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: when a person enters his house and mentions Allah’s name when entering and when eating, Satan says: you have no place to spend the night and no supper here. When he enters without mentioning Allah, Satan says: you have found a place to spend the night (Muslim 2018).
So a simple habit: say Bismillah when you come in, and when you start to eat. The next lesson in the app’s adhkar section has the full words for entering.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Waking each other for night prayer
body: Abu Huraira reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: may Allah have mercy on a man who gets up at night and prays, and wakes his wife; if she refuses, he sprinkles water on her face. May Allah have mercy on a woman who gets up at night and prays, and wakes her husband; if he refuses, she sprinkles water on his face (Abu Dawud 1308, graded hasan sahih by al-Albani).
It is mutual. Husband and wife encourage each other to the night prayer. The water is a gentle, playful picture, not force. If a spouse is ill, tired or has small children, kindness decides.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Abu Dawud 1308 (graded hasan sahih by al-Albani)

lessons.title: Forgiveness in the house
lessons.intro: Restraining anger, forgiving as Abu Bakr did, and a way to say sorry.

steps.title: Who says sorry first?
body: Anyone who has lived with other people knows the quiet that follows an argument. Both are waiting for the other to speak. This lesson is about breaking that silence, in a way that fits what the Qur’an and the Prophet ﷺ taught about forgiving.
It is for spouses, siblings, parents, children, and housemates.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.title: Restraining anger
steps.label: [Established]
steps.note: Allah describes the people of good: those who spend in ease and hardship, who restrain their anger, and who pardon people. He loves the doers of good. Forgiving begins with controlling the first reaction.

steps.title: The strong one
body: A man asked the Prophet ﷺ for advice. He said: do not become angry. The man asked again and again, and each time he said: do not become angry (Bukhari 6116). In another report the Prophet ﷺ said that the strong one is not the one who overcomes people by strength, but the one who controls himself in anger (Bukhari 6114).
So the first step is to pause. It is not weakness.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Abu Bakr and Mistah
body: During the slander against Aisha, Mistah, a poor relative whom Abu Bakr supported, joined those who spoke. Abu Bakr was hurt and swore to stop helping him. Then Allah revealed: do not let those of virtue and wealth among you swear not to give to relatives and the needy. Let them pardon and overlook. Would you not like that Allah should forgive you? (24:22).

Abu Bakr said: yes, by Allah, I would like that Allah forgive me. He gave Mistah his support again. Here the ayah asks a person to forgive someone who really hurt him, and links it to the hope that Allah will forgive us.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Forgiving raises you
body: The Prophet ﷺ said that charity does not reduce wealth, that no one forgives another except that Allah increases him in honour, and that no one humbles himself for Allah except that Allah raises him (Muslim 2588).
This is the opposite of what pride says. Pride says the one who says sorry first loses. The hadith says that forgiving earns honour with Allah.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Forgiving, and staying safe
steps.intro: Forgiveness is not the same as having no boundaries.
steps.agree: Pardon when you safely can, and seek help when you are not safe.

rows.name: Forgiving
rows.text: You can let go of the wish for revenge and leave the matter to Allah. 42:40 says that whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah.

rows.name: Staying safe
rows.text: Forgiving does not mean staying in a home where you are hurt. If someone is violent or abusive, protect yourself and seek help from trusted people.

rows.name: Fair settlement
rows.text: The same ayah allows a fair response to a wrong. Pardoning is better, but it is not a duty to put yourself in danger.

steps.closing: Forgive in the heart; protect yourself in practice.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: Please confirm that the framing of forgiveness versus safety in cases of abuse is acceptable and add a referral line if the app has one.

steps.title: The better one greets first
body: The Prophet ﷺ said it is not lawful for a Muslim to desert his brother for more than three nights, when they meet and turn away from each other, and the better of the two is the one who greets the other first (Bukhari 6077).

Scholars apply this to people who are on bad terms. A family member who is cross can use the same idea: greet first, and see how the other answers. Applying it to spouses is an application, not the exact wording of the hadith.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: The hadith is about brothers in Islam. The application to spouses and family members is an extension; please confirm the wording.

steps.text: Ask how to put it right.
steps.detail: What would help?

mistakes: Saying sorry only to end the argument.
Bringing up old arguments.
Waiting for the other to speak first.
